notes: True Whig Party (Tubman) in ruling slot 0; MD's slot-0 sprite belongs to Doe's NDPL, so icon null. MD's 1980s-2000s parties are anachronistic for 1970 and not used; only the AFL keeps its MD sprite (slot 22). Coalition slot 13 = the Executive Mansion apparatus around Secretary of State Rudolph Grimes. Tolbert placed via the Baptist Convention (slot 1).

0.name: True Whig Party
0.text:
The True Whig Party has ruled Liberia without interruption since 1878, the political machine of the Americo-Liberian elite. On 1 January 1970 its standard-bearer, William V. S. Tubman, President since 1944, has just begun his sixth term, with William R. Tolbert as Vice-President.

It stands for the Open Door Policy toward foreign investment, Tubman's Unification Policy toward the hinterland peoples and an unwavering alliance with the United States. Its base is the settler families, civil servants, chiefs and businessmen bound to it by patronage, and its leverage is total: no other party has won an election in nearly a century.

1.name: Liberia Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention
1.english: Liberia Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention
1.text:
The Liberia Baptist Missionary and Educational Convention unites the Baptist churches of the republic, one of the pillars of Americo-Liberian society. Its most prominent layman, Vice-President William R. Tolbert, has served as President of the Baptist World Alliance since 1965.

It stands for Christian civilization, mission schools, temperance and moral order, combined with a cautious reformism that hopes to modernize the True Whig state from within. Its base is churchgoers in Monrovia and the coastal counties, and its leverage lies in its schools, its pulpits and Tolbert's position as the likely successor.

2.name: Independent True Whig Party
2.text:
The Independent True Whig Party was formed in 1955 by former President Edwin Barclay to challenge Tubman's third-term ambitions. After its defeat and the assassination attempt of that year, it was crushed and its leaders prosecuted; on 1 January 1970 it survives only as a memory among old settler dissidents.

It stood for term limits, free elections, a free press and an end to one-man rule within the republic's own constitution. Its base is a few lawyers, editors and dissident settler families, and its leverage lies in the constitutional arguments that will resurface when Tubman's long rule ends.

3.name: The Harbel Strikers
3.text:
Harbel is the headquarters of the Firestone rubber plantation, the largest in the world and the biggest employer in Liberia. Strikes there and across the concessions in the 1960s were met with troops and new restrictions on unions; on 1 January 1970 the strikers' leaders are watched but not forgotten.

They want independent unions, higher wages, housing and schooling for tappers and their families, and enforcement of the labour laws on foreign concessions. Their base is plantation and mine workers and dockers, and their leverage lies in their power to halt the rubber and iron ore that fund the state.

4.name: Cuttington Study Circle
4.text:
Cuttington College in Suakoko is the Episcopal university of the interior, where some of the first hinterland students are encountering Marx and Lenin in borrowed pamphlets. On 1 January 1970 a small circle meets discreetly, aware that open communism is treason under Tubman.

They argue that Liberia is an American semi-colony and that only a vanguard party, nationalization of the concessions and an opening to the Soviet Union can end settler rule. Their base is a handful of students and young teachers, and their leverage lies in ideas that are beginning to spread among the educated youth of the hinterland.

5.name: Capitol Hill Radicals
5.text:
The University of Liberia on Capitol Hill in Monrovia is the training ground of the elite, but by 1970 its students are restless. Young radicals there read Fanon, Malcolm X and Nkrumah and discuss the Black Power movement in America and the liberation wars in Africa.

They denounce the settler oligarchy, foreign concessions and police spies, and call for democracy, land for the hinterland and a socialist future. Their base is students, young lecturers and returned graduates from America, and their leverage lies in campus agitation and their family ties to the very elite they attack.

6.name: Children of Garvey
6.text:
Marcus Garvey once dreamed of making Liberia the homeland of a Black empire, and his idea still resonates. On 1 January 1970 the Children of Garvey are a loose company of pan-Africanists, intellectuals and religious nationalists in Monrovia who see the republic as too close to Washington.

They stand for racial pride, an Africa united against Western domination, the rejection of American cultural influence and sympathy for the radical states of Guinea and Ghana's former leader Nkrumah. Their base is a small circle of writers, preachers and diaspora returnees, and their leverage lies in rhetoric that resonates with young people.

7.name: The PROs
7.text:
The 'Public Relations Officers' are Tubman's vast network of paid informers, planted in offices, schools, churches and markets across Liberia. On 1 January 1970 they report directly to the Executive Mansion on any whisper of dissent.

They stand for the absolute security of the President and his regime, preventive arrests and the silencing of critics. Their base is thousands of informers and security officials who owe their income to the system, and their leverage lies in fear, blackmail and their ability to destroy careers with a single report.

8.name: Monrovia's Shia Traders
8.text:
Liberia's Lebanese merchants, many of them Shia from southern Lebanon, run much of Monrovia's retail trade, though the constitution bars them from citizenship. On 1 January 1970 their elders look to Imam Musa al-Sadr and his new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

They favour a socially active, moderate Shia Islam built on schools and charities, and keep a low political profile while cultivating useful officials. Their base is shopkeepers, importers and their families, and their leverage lies in their grip on retail trade and the loans they make to the Liberian elite.

9.name: The Najaf Circle
9.text:
A few young Lebanese Shia from Monrovia study in the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini lectures on Islamic government. On 1 January 1970 their circle is tiny and inward-looking, centred on the community's prayer rooms.

They reject secular rule and Western influence and want clerics to guide the faithful in public life. Their base is devout youth and a handful of patrons, and their leverage lies in remittances and seminary networks that link West Africa to Iraq and Lebanon.

10.name: Mandingo Imams' Council
10.text:
The Mandingo Imams' Council gathers the imams and elders of Liberia's Mandingo and Vai Muslims, centred on the mosques of Monrovia, Lofa and Nimba. On 1 January 1970 they are a respected but politically marginal community in a state that defines itself as Christian.

They seek recognition of Islam, protection for Muslim traders, Quranic schools and pilgrimage support, and stay loyal to whoever governs. Their base is Mandingo traders and Vai Muslims, and their leverage lies in their trading networks across the Guinean and Sierra Leonean borders.

11.name: Lofa Wahhabiyya
11.text:
In Lofa County, near the Guinean border, returning pilgrims and traders influenced by the reformist Wahhabiyya of Kankan preach a stricter, scripture-centred Islam. On 1 January 1970 they are few, at odds with the established imams and with the traditional secret societies.

They condemn amulets, saint veneration and the Poro and Sande societies, and dream of Muslim communities governed by the Sharia rather than a Christian state. Their base is young Mandingo traders, and their leverage lies in cross-border trade and the resentment of Muslims excluded from Liberian power.

12.name: Monrovia Islamic Reformers
12.text:
The Monrovia Islamic Reformers are educated young Muslims who studied in Cairo or at mission schools and want their community to compete with the Christian elite. On 1 January 1970 they organize study groups and lobby for a Muslim school in the capital.

They promote modern Islamic education, social welfare, equal citizenship for Muslims and moral reform of public life, inspired by Egyptian reformist thought. Their base is young Mandingo and Vai professionals and traders, and their leverage lies in education and their links to the Arab world.

13.name: The Executive Mansion
13.text:
The new Executive Mansion, completed in 1964, is the centre of Tubman's personal rule, where cabinet members, county superintendents and chiefs come to receive orders and favours. On 1 January 1970 its key figure besides the President is Secretary of State Rudolph Grimes.

It stands for presidential supremacy, patronage, careful diplomacy between the blocs and the continuation of the Tubman system beyond Tubman. Its base is the cabinet, the presidential staff and the county superintendents, and its leverage lies in controlling every appointment, contract and budget in the republic.

14.name: The Hinterland Chiefs
14.text:
The paramount and clan chiefs of the Kpelle, Loma, Gio, Mano and other interior peoples administer the hinterland counties created under Tubman's Unification Policy. On 1 January 1970 they attend the President's Executive Councils and serve the True Whig state in return for recognition.

They defend customary law, land tenure, the Poro and Sande societies and their own authority against settler officials and young educated critics. Their base is the rural villages of the interior, and their leverage lies in their control over land, labour recruitment for the concessions and the rural vote.

15.name: Firestone Plantations Company
15.text:
Firestone has held its giant rubber concession at Harbel since 1926 under a 99-year agreement that shaped the modern Liberian state. On 1 January 1970 it remains the country's largest private employer and, with the iron mines, the backbone of the Open Door economy.

It wants stable concessions, low taxes, docile labour and an American-friendly government, and has long had a direct line to the Executive Mansion. Its base is American shareholders, plantation management and allied Liberian rubber farmers, and its leverage lies in the revenue and jobs no Liberian government can afford to lose.

16.name: The Open Door Merchants
16.text:
The Open Door Merchants are the importers, shipping agents and small entrepreneurs who thrive on Liberia's dollar economy and flag-of-convenience shipping registry. On 1 January 1970 they prosper in Monrovia's booming waterfront and resent the privileges of the settler families.

They want free trade, low tariffs, an end to the political favouritism that decides licences and contracts, and room for Liberian-owned business. Their base is traders, transport owners and professionals, and their leverage lies in the money they bring to the treasury and the US dollar that underpins the economy.

17.name: Mount Nimba Defenders
17.text:
On Mount Nimba, the LAMCO joint venture strips one of West Africa's richest iron ore deposits from a mountain famous for its unique wildlife. On 1 January 1970 a handful of scientists, teachers and local elders warn of the damage to forests and rivers.

They call for the protection of the Nimba highlands and the Sapo and Gola forests, controls on mining runoff and limits on logging concessions. Their base is foresters, missionaries and village communities near the mines, and their leverage lies in international scientific attention.

18.name: Kru Town Dockers
18.text:
The Kru seamen and dockers of Monrovia's Kru Town have worked West Africa's ships and ports for generations, and form the most organized section of the urban working class. On 1 January 1970 they are restive over wages and the domination of the port by foreign and settler interests.

They want fair wages, independent unions, cooperative ownership of fishing and port services and equal rights for indigenous Liberians. Their base is dockers, sailors and fishermen along the coast, and their leverage lies in their ability to shut down the Freeport of Monrovia.

19.name: The Little Red Book Circle
19.text:
Copies of Mao Zedong's quotations reach Monrovia through students and sailors, and a small circle has adopted them as a guide. On 1 January 1970 its members meet secretly, knowing that the PROs report on anything resembling communism.

They preach a peasant revolution of the hinterland against the settler elite and its American patrons, self-reliance and solidarity with liberation movements. Their base is a handful of students and young workers, and their leverage lies only in leaflets and the deep grievances of the interior.

20.name: Sons of the Soil
20.text:
The Sons of the Soil voice the anger of indigenous Liberians at a century of settler domination, forced labour scandals and exclusion from power. On 1 January 1970 their slogans spread among educated hinterland youth, soldiers and workers despite the Unification Policy.

They demand that the 'country people' rule their own country, end settler privilege and limit the role of Lebanese and foreign traders. Their base is indigenous students, junior soldiers and urban migrants, and their leverage lies in the sheer majority they represent.

21.name: The Old Settler Guard
21.text:
The Old Settler Guard are the hardline Americo-Liberian families who regard the republic as their inheritance and the hinterland peoples as subjects. On 1 January 1970 they fill the Masonic lodges, the Senate and the oldest True Whig circles of Monrovia.

They oppose any loosening of the settler monopoly on land, office and citizenship, and want harsher measures against dissent, unions and indigenous agitation. Their base is the old settler families of Montserrado and the coast, and their leverage lies in wealth, kinship and control over the legislature.

22.name: Armed Forces of Liberia
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Liberia were created in 1962 from the old Liberian Frontier Force and are trained and equipped by the United States. On 1 January 1970 their officers are largely settler appointees, while the rank and file are recruited from the indigenous peoples.

The army stands for order, loyalty to the President and close cooperation with America, but its soldiers resent poor pay and settler officers. Its base is the barracks of Monrovia and the interior garrisons, and its leverage lies in its monopoly on force.

23.name: Vai Kings of Grand Cape Mount
23.english: Vai Kings of Grand Cape Mount
23.text:
The Vai of Grand Cape Mount were ruled by kings long before the settlers arrived, and their ruling lineages, famous for the Vai script, still command respect. On 1 January 1970 they are paramount chiefs within the Liberian state, their royal titles recognized only by their own people.

Their supporters want hereditary rulers to regain dignity and authority alongside the republic, protecting Vai land, language and Islam. Their base is the Vai towns of the coast and their trading families, and their leverage lies in ancestral prestige.
